name: Agabus
title: The New Testament Prophet
summary: Agabus was a Christian prophet who served in the early church and is known for two significant prophecies recorded in Acts. He prophesied about a great famine that would strike the entire Roman world—a prophecy fulfilled during the reign of Emperor Claudius. Later, he warned the apostle Paul through a dramatic symbolic act that he would be bound and handed over to the Gentiles in Jerusalem. Agabus stands in the tradition of the Old Testament prophets and shows that the prophetic gift continued to operate in the early church.

keyEvents.title: The Prophecy of Famine
keyEvents.description: Agabus came down from Jerusalem to Antioch and prophesied by the Spirit that a great famine would come over the whole Roman world. This famine occurred during the reign of Emperor Claudius, which led the disciples in Antioch to send help to the believers in Judea.

keyEvents.title: The Warning to Paul in Caesarea
keyEvents.description: In Caesarea, at the house of the evangelist Philip, Agabus took Paul's belt and bound his own hands and feet in a symbolic prophetic act. He prophesied that the Jews in Jerusalem would bind the man who owned the belt and hand him over to the Gentiles. This dramatic sign-act stands in the tradition of Old Testament prophets like Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, who also used visual demonstrations to underscore their messages.

versions.summary: Agabus was a Christian prophet from Jerusalem known for two significant prophecies in the Acts of the Apostles. He prophesied about a great famine that would strike the whole world, and he warned the apostle Paul that he would be arrested in Jerusalem.
versions.title: The New Testament Prophet
versions.reason: [minor] The third event ('Symbolic prophetic action') overlaps significantly with the second event ('The warning to Paul in Caesarea') and refers to the same verse (Acts 21:11). The symbolic action is already described in the second event. It may be considered whether this should be merged with the second event to avoid redundancy, or alternatively given a more distinct angle.; [minor] The summary states that Agabus was 'from Jerusalem', but the text in Acts 11:27 says only that he came down from Jerusalem to Antioch. This does not necessarily mean he was from Jerusalem – he may have been staying there. A more precise formulation would be 'a Christian prophet who came from Jerusalem'.; [major] There are no footnotes covering interesting historical, linguistic, or theological details. For example: the historical famine under Claudius, parallels of the prophetic action to OT prophets, and the Greek name Agabus.

footnotes.text: The famine Agabus prophesied is historically confirmed. The Roman historian Josephus (Antiquitates Judaicae 20.2.5; 20.5.2) describes a severe famine in Judea around AD 46–48, during the reign of Emperor Claudius (AD 41–54). Roman authors such as Suetonius and Cassius Dio also mention food shortages in the Roman Empire during this period.

Agabus's symbolic act of binding his own hands and feet with Paul's belt stands in a long tradition of prophetic sign-acts known from the Old Testament. Prophets like Isaiah (Isa 20:2–4), Jeremiah (Jer 13:1–11; 27:2), and Ezekiel (Ezek 4:1–3; 12:3–7) used similar dramatic demonstrations to give their messages visual and emotional impact.

The name 'Agabus' (Greek: Ἄγαβος, Hagabos) is possibly derived from the Hebrew name Hagab (חָגָב), which means 'locust'. A similar name appears in Ezra 2:46, where Hagab is mentioned among the descendants of the temple servants who returned from exile.

In early Christian tradition, Agabus was counted among the seventy disciples whom Jesus sent out (Luke 10:1). This tradition is found, among others, in Pseudo-Hippolytus (a work on the seventy apostles) and in Byzantine menologia. There is no New Testament confirmation of this, but it testifies that Agabus was highly regarded in the early church.
